To ascertain something means to find out a fact with certainty through deliberate effort. When you ascertain something, you don't stumble upon it by accident — you actively investigate, check, or inquire until you can say with confidence that you know it.

A simple way to picture it: imagine you want to know if a train is running on time. You could guess, or you could check the app and know for sure. That act of checking — the deliberate effort that takes you from "I don't know" to "I know for certain" — is what ascertain captures.
The Two Ideas Hidden Inside This One Word

Ascertain quietly carries two ideas at the same time, and both matter.

The first is effort. You didn't passively receive the information. You went looking for it — you investigated, asked, examined, or tested. The second is certainty. You didn't end up with a guess or a hunch. You ended up with a confirmed, reliable fact.

This is what makes ascertain richer than the casual phrase "find out." "Find out" is neutral and everyday. Ascertain signals that you made a deliberate, careful effort and arrived at something confirmed and dependable.
How It Works in a Sentence

Ascertain is always followed by what you found out. That "what" can take two forms.

It can be a noun or noun phrase: "She ascertained the cause of the fire." Or it can be a clause introduced by words like whether, if, what, who, when, or how: "She ascertained whether the building was safe."

You would not say "She ascertained the building is safe" — you need that connecting word to link ascertain to a full idea.

• A doctor runs tests to ascertain the cause of a patient's symptoms.
  • The detective interviewed every witness to ascertain who had entered the building that night.
  • Before approving the plan, the manager needed to ascertain whether the budget was sufficient.
  • The inspector ascertained that the bridge met all safety requirements.
  • Please ascertain the exact deadline before submitting the application.

Notice the pattern in every case: there is a question that needs answering, there is an effort to answer it, and the result is a definite, confirmed piece of knowledge — not a guess.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close neighbours, but they are not identical.

Find out is the casual, everyday version. "I found out the answer." Ascertain is more formal and implies greater care and rigour.

Discover often suggests something new or surprising coming to light — sometimes even by chance. Ascertain is always intentional; there is nothing accidental about it.

Verify means to check something you already believe or suspect is true. Ascertain is more open-ended — you start from a place of not knowing and work toward knowing.

Confirm is similar to verify. You already have a belief, and confirmation makes sure it's right. With ascertain, you're not starting with a prior belief at all.

Determine is the closest word of all. Both mean to find something out definitively. The difference is subtle: "determine" is slightly more common in everyday use, while "ascertain" carries a slightly more formal, investigative, or official tone. In many sentences, the two are interchangeable.
When to Use It (and When Not To)

Ascertain is a formal word. It fits naturally in legal writing ("The court must ascertain the facts before ruling"), investigative or journalistic contexts, academic papers, official reports, and professional communication.

In casual conversation, it sounds stiff. You would not say "Let me ascertain whether the pizza has arrived" — you'd simply say "Let me check if the pizza's here." But in a formal report or a legal document, ascertain fits perfectly and sounds authoritative.

Ascertain does not mean to guess — guessing gives you a possibility; ascertaining gives you a confirmed fact. It does not mean to assume — assumptions are not verified, but ascertained facts are. And it is never passive. You cannot ascertain something by accident. There is always a conscious, deliberate act of inquiry involved.
A Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture a detective at a crime scene. They do not guess who did it. They collect clues, question people, examine evidence, and piece things together — until they know for certain. That entire journey from "I don't know" to "I know for certain, because I did the work to find out" — that is what it means to ascertain something.
